methods: identifier-level inventory across the two forks before scoping (19 epure-only identifiers, only 4 crossing)
checked for an injection seam and an integration harness before declaring the items untestable, rather than assuming
suggestion: roster-run's Fast/Full classifier asks 'what to build vs how'. A third question would have caught this earlier: 'can each change be proven by a test that fails first?' An unprovable change in Fast mode is a Full-mode design question about testability, not an implementation detail.

frictions: The skill's questions.md template mandates '# Research Questions — <task-slug>' while the same skill requires zero intent disclosure. For a descriptive slug (here: port-fork-robustness-fixes) the title briefs the blind researcher on exactly what the file exists to hide. Deviated deliberately and recorded the reason in the file itself.
methods: greped the produced questions for goal vocabulary before presenting them, rather than trusting the generator to have stayed neutral — 4 hits, 3 were regex noise (re-exported, transport, fixture) and 1 was the mandated title
suggestion: Either drop the slug from the questions.md title, or have roster-question derive a neutral title from the domain (e.g. '# Research Questions — language-server extraction') while the filename keeps the slug. The filename is not read by the researcher; the title is.

frictions: The scoping inventory compared the two forks by IDENTIFIER, not by behaviour: it grepped for `partial_fns` (a name chosen in the other codebase) and read its absence as the absence of honest-partial-results, which this repo already implements as `fn_rows_ref`. Two of four items evaporated on first contact with the code.

A grep for 'ocamllsp|run_lsp|OCAMLLSP' over test/ tezt/ returned nothing and was read as 'no LSP test harness exists'. The harness exists (tezt/tests/lsp_readiness.ml) — a STUB server does not mention ocamllsp, and it drives the CLI binary rather than run_lsp. Third absence-from-a-bounded-search in one session.

The first version of the diagnostics test asserted the sentinel appeared SOMEWHERE in the output. The stub refuses every request, so a second site surfaced the same sentinel and the mutation removing the first diagnostic SURVIVED. The test passed for the wrong reason and would have shipped as proof.
methods: red observed before every fix, with the exit code recorded, not asserted
every mutation run through `dune test` rather than by invoking a test binary — the shortcut that invalidated a mutation table earlier this week
reused the repo's own stub-server pattern instead of designing a seam, once research found it
suggestion: roster-question/research should carry an explicit instruction to compare BEHAVIOUR across forks, not identifiers — 'grep the name' is the default move and it is wrong whenever the two sides were written by different hands. A one-line rule in roster-research ('an identifier's absence is not a behaviour's absence; find the behaviour') would have saved this task two phases.

frictions: Both available secondary runtimes degraded with reason=tree-mutation, runtime_exit=3, on the same prompt (digest f351472844ff5fea). codex applied the M1 mutation from the brief's mutation table (removing the absolutisation in file_uri_of_path); opencode deleted 9 lines from lsp_extractor.ml, i.e. one of the new diagnostics. Neither reported a finding. So the mandatory cross-runtime pass is structurally unavailable here, not merely flaky: 2 of 2 runtimes reproduce the experiments described in the prompt instead of reporting observations about them.

Hypothesis worth testing before blaming the runtimes: the prompt embeds the impl brief, which contains a mutation table naming exact code edits (M1..M5). A runtime given write access and a list of mutations may reasonably read it as work to perform. The wrapper's tree-integrity snapshot caught it both times, which is the safeguard working.
methods: restored the tree after each degraded run and verified `git diff HEAD --stat` was empty before continuing, rather than trusting the wrapper's cleanup
inspected what each runtime mutated before discarding its output — the mutation itself is information even when the findings are void
suggestion: xruntime-review should either strip mutation-table-like sections from the prompt it forwards, or state in the forwarded prompt that the runtime has read-only intent and any edit voids the run. Right now the prompt hands a runtime an explicit list of code edits and then fails it for making them.
